items.title: The Bay of Pigs invasion (April 1961) was a CIA-trained failure
items.claim: What happened at the Bay of Pigs?

options.text: A successful US Marine landing in Cuba

Around 1,400 CIA-trained Cuban exiles (Brigade 2506) landed at Bahía de Cochinos on 17 April 1961; without expected US air support, they were defeated within three days, with 114 killed and around 1,200 captured
A peaceful protest broken up by Castro's police

items.reveal:
The operation was planned under Eisenhower and inherited by Kennedy after his January 1961 inauguration. Kennedy cancelled the second air strike that would have neutralised Cuban air power. The exiles landed in swampy terrain with no popular uprising materialising.

Kennedy publicly accepted responsibility — 'success has many fathers, failure is an orphan' — and the CIA director Allen Dulles resigned. The prisoners were exchanged in December 1962 for $53 million of food and medicine.

The humiliation pushed Castro further toward the Soviet Union; Khrushchev's decision to place missiles in Cuba in 1962 followed directly. Operation Mongoose continued covert efforts against Castro through the 1960s.
items.why: Failed interventions can be more consequential than successful ones. The Bay of Pigs led directly to the Cuban Missile Crisis — and reshaped Cold War risk-taking for both sides.

items.title: The US Vietnam draft was decided by a televised lottery
items.claim: How was the Vietnam draft (Selective Service) administered after 1969?

options.text: Strict order by date of birth, alphabetical
On 1 December 1969, blue capsules with birthdates were drawn from a glass jar on national TV — men born on dates drawn first were called up first
By state quota with each state choosing its own method

items.reveal:
The 1 December 1969 lottery selected 19-26 year olds. 366 capsules (one per birthday including 29 February) were drawn live. Men with low numbers (1-195) were called; high numbers (typically 196+) were spared.

The statistical method was later shown to have biased the draw — capsules added in order from January were less thoroughly mixed, so December birthdays were over-represented at low numbers.

Deferments before 1969 — for university students, for medical reasons — disproportionately spared the wealthy. Around 2.7 million Americans served in Vietnam; 58,220 died. The draft ended in 1973.
items.why: Even apparently neutral mechanisms encode injustice. The Vietnam draft's class bias before 1969, and the statistical bias of the 1969 lottery itself, are case studies in how 'fairness' breaks down in practice.

items.title: The Berlin Wall fell partly because of a press-conference error
items.claim: How did the Berlin Wall come to open on 9 November 1989?

options.text: Soviet troops dismantled it overnight on Gorbachev's orders

East German official Günter Schabowski announced new travel rules at a 6 p.m. press conference; asked when they took effect, he said 'as far as I know, immediately'; East Berliners massed at checkpoints and crossings opened without orders
Mass armed insurrection overwhelmed border guards
West German forces breached the wall by force

items.reveal:
The East German politburo had agreed new travel rules on 9 November 1989, intended to take effect the following day with bureaucratic processing. Schabowski had not been briefed in detail. Asked by Italian journalist Riccardo Ehrman 'when does this take effect?', he shuffled papers and said 'Sofort, unverzüglich' — immediately, without delay.

Within hours East Berliners gathered at the Bornholmer Strasse crossing. Commander Harald Jäger received no orders and, faced with thousands of citizens, opened the barrier around 11.30 p.m.

Within months the regime collapsed. German reunification followed on 3 October 1990. The Soviet Union itself dissolved on 26 December 1991.
items.why: Major historical turning points can hinge on a botched press conference. The Wall's opening was not authorised in the way it happened — it was triggered by a misstatement that the crowd then made real.
